text: The atmosphere has a mass of a little over five quadrillion tonnes, about 5.15e18 kg.
as_written: a little over five quadrillion tonnes
source: Trenberth and Smith 2005, 'The Mass of the Atmosphere', Journal of Climate; NCAR Climate Data Guide

text: The atmosphere's mass is under one millionth of Earth's mass (about 5.15e18 kg versus 5.97e24 kg).
as_written: less than one millionth of the mass of the Earth
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (Earth mass 5.97e24 kg); Trenberth and Smith 2005

text: Mars lost most of its atmosphere over billions of years, as found by MAVEN.
as_written: took billions of years to do it, according to NASA's MAVEN mission
source: NASA MAVEN mission results (Jakosky et al., Science 2017)

text: Sea-level air pressure is about 101,325 pascals, equivalent to about ten tonnes of weight per square metre.
as_written: about ten tonnes on every square metre
source: International Standard Atmosphere (ISO 2533 / ICAO Doc 7488)

text: Ten tonnes of force per square metre acts on walls, windows and roofs when outside pressure is zero and inside is one atmosphere.
as_written: ten tonnes of force pushing outward
source: International Standard Atmosphere (ISO 2533); simple pressure-times-area calculation

text: Solar irradiance above the atmosphere is about 1361 watts per square metre.
as_written: about thirteen hundred and sixty one watts on every square metre
source: Kopp and Lean 2011, SORCE Total Irradiance Monitor

text: Clear-sky sea-level sunlight on a surface facing the sun is roughly 1000 watts per square metre.
as_written: roughly a thousand
source: ASTM G173 / NREL standard solar spectrum, AM1.5

text: The ozone layer absorbs the shortest, most damaging ultraviolet radiation.
as_written: The ozone layer normally absorbs the shortest ultraviolet
source: WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion

text: Divers can suffer lung overpressure injury from ascents of only a metre or two while holding their breath.
as_written: a metre or two of ascent
source: US Navy Diving Manual, pulmonary barotrauma section; Divers Alert Network
second_opinion_reason: Pulmonary barotrauma generally requires an ascent of several feet to tens of feet with a closed glottis, but standard diving physiology and safety guidelines typically cite a risk threshold starting around 4 feet (about 1.2 metres) under specific conditions; however, a strict 1-to-2 metre limit without caveats is slightly exaggerated as a general rule for lung overpressure.

text: The vapour pressure of water at body temperature is about 6.3 kilopascals.
as_written: about six point three kilopascals
source: NIST Chemistry WebBook / standard steam tables; Armstrong limit definition

text: 6.3 kilopascals is about six percent of standard sea-level pressure of 101.3 kilopascals.
as_written: about six percent of normal sea level pressure
source: Arithmetic from ISO 2533 and NIST water vapour pressure data

text: Air pressure falls to the Armstrong limit at an altitude of roughly 19 kilometres.
as_written: roughly nineteen kilometres
source: Ernsting's Aviation and Space Medicine; NASA/FAA descriptions of the Armstrong limit

text: In 1965 at NASA Johnson Space Center, Jim LeBlanc was exposed to near vacuum in a suit failure and stayed conscious about 14 seconds.
as_written: In 1965, at NASA's Johnson Space Center
source: NASA Johnson Space Center accounts of the 1965 vacuum chamber accident; Landis 2007, 'Human Exposure to Vacuum'

text: LeBlanc remained conscious for about 14 seconds.
as_written: about fourteen seconds
source: NASA Johnson Space Center accounts of the 1965 vacuum chamber accident

text: Time of useful consciousness above about 15 km (50,000 ft) is roughly 9 to 12 seconds.
as_written: roughly nine to twelve seconds
source: FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute, time of useful consciousness table

text: The altitude above which that consciousness time applies is about 15 kilometres (50,000 feet).
as_written: above about fifteen kilometres
source: FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute

text: Airliners cruise at about 11 kilometres altitude (around 35,000 feet).
as_written: about eleven kilometres
source: FAA / ICAO typical cruise altitudes

text: Free fall for 10 seconds covers about 490 metres (0.5 x 9.81 x 100).
as_written: about four hundred and ninety metres
source: Standard gravity 9.80665 m/s2, kinematics

text: After 10 seconds of free fall, speed is about 98 metres per second.
as_written: about ninety-eight metres per second
source: Standard gravity 9.80665 m/s2, kinematics

text: 98 metres per second is about 350 kilometres per hour.
as_written: close to three hundred and fifty kilometres per hour
source: Unit conversion of 98 m/s

text: The atmosphere's weight equals about 10 metres of seawater, and pressure doubles at about 10 metres depth.
as_written: roughly ten metres deep
source: NOAA Ocean Service; US Navy Diving Manual

text: Pressure doubles when you dive about ten metres.
as_written: pressure doubles when you dive ten metres
source: NOAA Ocean Service; US Navy Diving Manual

text: Water at ordinary sea temperatures has a vapour pressure of roughly 1.7 kPa, which is matched by about 17 centimetres of water depth, so boiling is suppressed below roughly a quarter of a metre.
as_written: less than a quarter of a metre
source: NIST water vapour pressure data; hydrostatic pressure calculation

text: A diver ten metres down experiences about one atmosphere of absolute pressure when the atmosphere is absent, equal to normal sea level now.
as_written: under about the pressure of an ordinary day on land
source: Hydrostatic pressure calculation; US Navy Diving Manual

text: Earth without its greenhouse effect would have an effective temperature of about minus 18 degrees Celsius.
as_written: about minus eighteen degrees Celsius
source: NASA Earth Observatory; IPCC AR4 Working Group 1 FAQ 1.1

text: That is about 33 degrees colder than the actual average surface temperature of about 15 degrees Celsius.
as_written: around thirty-three degrees colder than today
source: NASA Earth Observatory; IPCC AR4 Working Group 1 FAQ 1.1

text: The heat capacity of the whole atmosphere equals that of only the top few metres of the ocean.
as_written: The top few metres of the ocean hold as much heat as the whole atmosphere above them
source: Calculation from atmospheric mass per area (about 10,300 kg/m2, Trenberth and Smith 2005) and specific heats from NIST; standard textbook result

text: Three Soyuz 11 cosmonauts died in 1971 when their capsule depressurised in space.
as_written: Soyuz 11 in 1971, when three cosmonauts died
source: NASA NSSDCA Soyuz 11 mission record; Roscosmos history

text: World population is about eight billion.
as_written: Eight billion people
source: United Nations World Population Prospects 2022; UN announcement of 15 November 2022

text: A car at 100 km/h covers about 278 metres in ten seconds.
as_written: two hundred and seventy-eight metres
source: Arithmetic: 100 km/h = 27.8 m/s

text: Fossil fuels supply well over half of global electricity (about 60 percent in 2023).
as_written: well over half of the world's electricity
source: Ember Global Electricity Review 2024; IEA Electricity 2024

text: Tardigrades were exposed to open space for ten days in 2007 and many survived.
as_written: exposed to the vacuum of open space for ten days
source: Jonsson et al. 2008, Current Biology, FOTON-M3 mission, ESA

text: Lichens on the outside of the ISS spent about 1.5 years in space and recovered.
as_written: about a year and a half in space
source: ESA EXPOSE-E experiment on the ISS, 2008 to 2009

text: Plants account for about 450 gigatonnes of carbon out of roughly 550 gigatonnes in all living things.
as_written: about four hundred and fifty billion tonnes out of roughly five hundred and fifty billion tonnes
source: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018, PNAS, 'The biomass distribution on Earth'

text: Bacteria account for about 70 gigatonnes of carbon.
as_written: Bacteria come in at about seventy billion
source: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018, PNAS

text: All animals total about 2 gigatonnes of carbon, under half a percent of global biomass.
as_written: about two billion tonnes, less than half a percent of the living mass of the planet
source: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018, PNAS

text: The census of life by carbon mass was published in 2018.
as_written: A 2018 census of life on Earth
source: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018, PNAS
